rationale: Citation counts in section 5 match data/lit/openalex-records-summary.json and studies/_shared/openalex_probe.py: median 8, mean 36.29, 90th percentile 75, maximum 2937, 284 zeros, 1790 of 1805 PMIDs. The frozen snapshot exists. Direction has not been crossed with citations, so this is not a look at the hypothesis of the P01v2 kind. The kappa stop is written before any labels. Those parts hold. The primary analysis does not. Section 2's single incidence rate ratio cannot be read from a four-level direction variable whose mixed and not-applicable levels have no stated fate in the glm.nb. topic_block and journal_size are not defined, and 1009 of 1830 labelled records carry two or more topic labels. The 76 percent figure used to keep 2025 and 2026 papers is the 2020-onward share (1375 of 1805 PMIDs), not the 2025-2026 share (484 of 1805, 26.8 percent). Of 284 zeros, 221 are from 2025-2026, so most zeros are papers with almost no time at risk, not papers nobody used. The citation tail that motivates quantile regression includes phrase-matched methods reviews, science-of-science surveys, and a clinical meta-analysis, not only verdicts that a practice is inadequate. I did not find a published study that already runs this exact contrast on meta-research articles. Duyx et al. 2017 (PMID 28603008) is the citation-bias review this question belongs to and is not cited. Serra-Garcia and Gneezy 2021 (PMID 34020944) is related and studies a different population.

findings.problem: The primary null is a single incidence rate ratio for conclusion direction. The exposure instrument in section 6 has four labels (inadequate, adequate, mixed, not applicable) and section 7 enters direction as one term in glm.nb. A four-level factor in that model yields three coefficients, not one IRR. Mixed and not applicable have no stated coding, reference level, or exclusion rule. Not applicable is not a spare bin: the unscreened tier A query admits methods papers, science-of-science reviews, and clinical articles that only use a query phrase, so a large share of the 1790 rows may be not applicable. Until those rows are dropped or separately modeled, the coefficient named in section 2 does not exist, and probe PC cannot compute a detectable rate ratio for the contrast the hypothesis actually states.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Define the primary estimand as the negative-binomial IRR for inadequate versus adequate. Exclude mixed and not applicable from that model and report their counts. Name the reference level. If mixed is retained, specify the dummy coding and which coefficient is the primary test. Recompute PC on the inadequate-versus-adequate split only, after the 300 labels exist.
findings.quote: The incidence rate ratio for conclusion direction is 1.

findings.problem: The protocol keeps 2025 and 2026 articles because excluding them would drop 76 percent of the corpus. That number is false for the window named in the sentence. Among the 1805 PMID records, 484 are from 2025-2026 (26.8 percent). The 76 percent figure is the 2020-onward share (1375 of 1805; 1396 of 1830 in MAP.md). The same error appears in the OpenAlex matches: 482 of 1790 are from 2025-2026 (26.9 percent), 1369 of 1790 from 2020 onward (76.5 percent). The false percentage is what justifies keeping 223 matched 2026 papers whose median citation count is 0.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Replace 76 percent with the computed 2025-2026 share (about 27 percent). If the scientific reason to keep brand-new papers is not that share, say the real reason. If 2026 papers are kept, treat their zeros as time-at-risk, not as unused papers, and recompute the section 5 distribution with and without them.
findings.quote: Articles from 2025 and 2026 are retained and age is modeled, not trimmed; excluding recent work would drop 76 percent of the corpus.

findings.problem: Zeros are retained because a zero means nobody used the paper. On the frozen OpenAlex snapshot that sentence is mostly false. 161 of 223 matched 2026 papers have zero citations, and 60 of 259 matched 2025 papers do. That is 221 of the 284 zeros (77.8 percent). For those rows a zero is the expected count after a few months of indexing, not evidence of non-use. Dropping zeros would still condition on the outcome for older papers; keeping 2026 zeros folds a pile of structural zeros into the negative-binomial dispersion. The justification in the threats table (Removed) therefore overstates what was fixed.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Split zeros by years since publication. Keep old zeros as informative. For papers from 2025-2026, either exclude them from the primary count model, use an explicit time offset or hurdle on papers with at least one full year of follow-up, or model time to first citation. Do not describe 2026 zeros as papers nobody used.
findings.quote: 284 articles have zero citations. They are retained; a zero is informative about a paper nobody used and dropping them would condition on the outcome.

findings.problem: Section 5 computes the citation distribution on all 1790 matches and then says the incentive argument lives in the tail, which is why quantile regression is fitted. That tail is not a tail of verdicts about research practice. The maximum of 2937 is Deeks et al. 2003 (PMID 14499048), an HTA methods review that matched because the abstract contains meta-epidemiological techniques. Also in the top 15: Fortunato et al. 2018 Science of science (phrase match); Roberts et al. 2020 on racial inequality in psychology (mentions metascience); Simons et al. 2017 COG (keyword meta-science); Huang et al. 2020 on gender and scientific careers (science of science); Fazel et al. 2012 on violence in psychosis (PMID 23418482), a clinical systematic review whose abstract says a novel meta-epidemiological approach was used to group similar risk. Wood 2008 and Smaldino 2016 are on-target and also sit in that tail. The mixture was visible in the frozen file when the tail analysis was written, and before any not-applicable label exists to remove the off-target rows.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Do not choose quantile regression from the unscreened citation distribution. After the 300 labels, recompute the citation distribution inside inadequate, adequate, mixed, and not applicable. If the upper tail is mostly not applicable, drop the claim that the incentive lives in that tail, and make the primary estimand a contrast among papers that actually issue a verdict.
findings.quote: The incentive argument lives in the tail and a mean effect would not find it.

findings.problem: The same paragraph that specifies glm.nb as the primary model says a mean effect would not find the incentive. Negative binomial regression with a log link is a model for the conditional mean. With right-skewed citations the mean is already tail-sensitive (mean 36.29 versus median 8). If the scientific claim is a shift only in the upper quantiles, the primary estimand is the 90th-percentile contrast, not the NB IRR. As written, a null on the primary model could be read as no incentive while the text already says that model is the wrong place to look.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Pick one primary estimand and stick to it. If the hypothesis is a mean count ratio after age, journal, and topic adjustment, drop the sentence that a mean effect would not find it. If the hypothesis is a tail incentive, make the 90th-percentile quantile regression primary and treat glm.nb as secondary.
findings.quote: The incentive argument lives in the tail and a mean effect would not find it.

findings.problem: The hypothesis says the comparison is adjusted for journal. The model adjusts for journal_size, which is never defined. OpenAlex probe fields do not include a venue-size or impact-factor series, so journal_size is not a computed variable in the frozen snapshot. If it means count of corpus papers per journal, 428 of 639 journals in the PMID sample are singletons and the covariate is mostly 1. If it means journal identity, 639 levels on 1790 rows is not the formula as written. topic_block is likewise undefined. Labels in records-labelled.jsonl are multi-label: 1009 of 1830 records carry two or more topics, 11 carry none. A single factor cannot be formed without a rule that is not in the protocol. The fitted coefficient on direction is therefore not the adjusted IRR described in section 2.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Define journal_size as a named, dated variable (for example OpenAlex source citedness, or 2025 Scopus CiteScore) retrieved into the snapshot. If the adjustment is journal identity, say so and use a random intercept or a collapsed size band; do not claim journal adjustment for a size proxy. Define topic_block as a mutually exclusive rule (primary label, or a pre-specified hierarchy) and report how many records are multi-label under that rule. Fit the unadjusted model as already promised in section 8.

findings.problem: What would falsify the hypothesis is an interval containing 1. No interval, alpha, or smallest interesting rate ratio is named. Probe PC, which would say what rate ratio the realized split can detect, is outstanding and depends on the exposure split that does not yet exist. A wide interval containing 1 is non-rejection, not falsification of a directional claim that inadequate papers accrue more citations. The interesting alternative is IRR greater than 1; an interval such as 0.9 to 2.5 contains 1 and still includes a large incentive. This is the same class of null overclaim P01v2 made with a computed power grid; here the grid has not even been computed.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Name a 95 percent CI as the interval. State a smallest IRR that would still matter. Falsify the directional claim only if the CI lies entirely below 1, or run an equivalence test against the margin PC says is detectable. Do not treat a CI that contains 1 as a negative methodological result until PC is in the protocol.

findings.problem: The protocol frames the question as publication bias moved to the citation stage and does not cite the citation-bias literature. Duyx, Urlings, Swaen, Bouter, and Zeegers, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 2017, PMID 28603008, reviewed 52 studies and found statistically significant articles cited 1.6 times as often (95 percent CI 1.3 to 1.8) and articles whose authors concluded support for their hypothesis cited 2.7 times as often (CI 2.0 to 3.7). Jannot, Agoritsas, Gayet-Ageron, and Perneger, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 2013, PMID 23257169, found significant studies cited about twice as often, with much of the association running through journal impact factor. That literature says positive and hypothesis-supporting results are cited more, not less. In meta-research, concluding that a practice is inadequate is often the result the authors sought, so inadequate may be the field's positive finding. If so, P03 is a population-specific test of ordinary citation bias, not an inverted publication-bias mechanism. Serra-Garcia and Gneezy, Science Advances 2021, PMID 34020944, found nonreplicable original papers cited more than replicable ones; that is a different population (original findings, not meta-research conclusions) and is also uncited. I did not find a study that already classifies meta-research conclusions as inadequate versus adequate and models OpenAlex or Web of Science counts on that split.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Cite Duyx 2017 and Jannot 2013 as citation bias, not publication bias at the citation stage. State whether inadequate is coded as bad news or as support for a problem-finding hypothesis. Distinguish Serra-Garcia and Gneezy 2021 as related work on a different unit. Keep the claim of novelty only for the meta-research-conclusion contrast, which I could not find already done.
findings.quote: This is publication bias asked about the field that studies publication bias, and asked at the citation stage rather than at acceptance.

findings.problem: The reference standard is 300 author labels on abstracts. Three gaps make that instrument fail to measure the exposure in section 2 for the sample in section 4. First, 112 of 1805 PMID records have no abstract (108 of the 1790 OpenAlex matches). Classification of abstracts cannot be extended to those rows, and the protocol never mentions them. Second, stratified is unspecified: not by year, topic, journal, citation quartile, or publication type. A validation sample that is light on the citation tail or on not-applicable methods papers will not estimate the error that matters for section 5. Third, the author wrote the hypothesis that bad news is cited more and is not blinded to fame or to the frozen citation file. Highly cited phrase matches (Deeks 2003, Wood 2008, Smaldino 2016, Fortunato 2018) are recognizable. Outcome-contaminated gold labels will inflate kappa and bake the hypothesis into the instrument. Kappa 0.70 on four classes can also be carried by agreement on not applicable while inadequate versus adequate, the actual contrast, remains noisy.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Restrict the analysis set to records with an abstract, or specify a full-text rule for the rest, and recompute section 5 on that set. Pre-specify the stratification factors and include citation-quartile and publication-type strata. Blind the author to citation counts, journal, year, and title when labelling, presenting abstract text only. Report kappa for the binary inadequate-versus-adequate contrast among applicable records, not only the four-class kappa, and gate on that binary agreement.
findings.quote: A stratified random sample of **300 abstracts is classified by the author** into inadequate, adequate, mixed, or not applicable.

findings.problem: The banner states the protocol is not registered. Section 7 then calls the quantile regressions and the dual-classifier models preregistered. Probe PA had already returned the skewed citation distribution (mean 36.29, median 8, maximum 2937) on 2026-09-16, and sections 5 and 7 chose negative binomial plus upper-tail quantile regression because of that distribution. Those analysis choices were made after seeing the outcome, then labelled preregistered. That is not registration, and it is not a plan written before the outcome was inspected.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Delete preregistered until an independent registry record exists. Say specified in this protocol after the citation probe. If quantile regression is retained, state that it was chosen after inspecting the unscreened citation distribution and is therefore not a pre-outcome commitment.
findings.quote: Preregistered alongside: quantile regression at the 75th and 90th percentiles,

findings.problem: The stated OpenAlex n is 1790 works from 1805 PMIDs. The jsonl has 1790 unique OpenAlex IDs but only 1789 unique PMIDs. PMID 42018420 is two works with the same DOI, citation counts 3 and 0. The match rate is therefore 1789 unique PMIDs of 1805 (99.1 percent), and the 284 zeros include that extra zero row.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Deduplicate on PMID or DOI before computing match rate and citation summaries. Report 1789 matched PMIDs and recompute the table.
findings.quote: 1790 of 1805 tier A PMIDs resolved in OpenAlex, a match rate of 99.2 percent.

findings.problem: Section 5 says quantile regression is fitted on the upper deciles. Section 7 specifies the 75th and 90th percentiles. The 75th percentile is not an upper decile.
findings.what_would_fix_it: Name the quantiles once. If 75th and 90th, do not call them the upper deciles.
findings.quote: a quantile regression on the upper deciles is fitted alongside
